items.title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
items.summary: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolut
items.content: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, He
items.author: Mamoona Tasadduq, Maryam Bashir

items.title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Agnostic PAC Learning for Partial Concept Classes
items.summary: Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$. items.content: Let $\mathcal H\subseteq\{-1,+1,\star\}^{\mathcal X}$ be a partial concept class of finite VC dimension $d$. We construct a deterministic agnostic PAC learner that, for every $\varepsilon,δ\in(0,1)$, uses $O((d+\log(1/δ))/\varepsilon^2)$ i.i.d. examples from an arbitrary distribution $\mathcal D$ over $\mathcal X\times\{-1,+1\}$ and returns a total concept $\hat h:\mathcal X\to\{-1,+1\}$ satisfying $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(\hat h)\leq \min_{h\in\mathcal H}\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)+\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-δ$, where $\text{er}_{\mathcal D}(h)=\mathbb P_{(x,y)\sim\mathcal D}[h(x)\neq y]$. This establishes the optimal sample complexity, matching the lower bound of Alon et al. (FOCS 2021).

items.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) exhibit strong semantic understanding but remain limited in their ability to reason about metric 3D space in the physical world. Existing VLMs typically infer 3D scene structure from one or more images without known camera calibration or cross-view geometric constraints. This makes metric 3D inference inherently ambiguous and leaves it unclear whether their spatial predictions are grounded in visual evidence or driven primarily by semantic priors. In contrast, calibrated stereo provides explicit cross-view geometry that resolves this ambiguity and offers a more reliable foundation for metric 3D perception and geometric generalization. items.content: Detecting individual instances is crucial for many segmentation problems. However, expert instance annotations are often unavailable, so instances are approximated heuristically (e.g., as connected components of semantic maps), which can merge touching objects or split fragmented ones. Even when expert annotations exist, expert disagreement or structural delineation biases can yield split or merged reference instances, corresponding to over- or under-segmentation, respectively. Panoptic Quality (PQ) and related metrics capture both segmentation and detection quality while weighting all instances equally, regardless of size. items.content: Electronic health records (EHRs) contain rich health information for uncovering latent patient representations and clinically meaningful subgroups. Learning from EHR data across institutions is valuable because representations learned at a single site may reflect local data patterns and lack generalizability, yet pooling patient-level records across institutions is often impractical because of privacy constraints and communication costs. We propose a communication-efficient, non-iterative federated spectral method for learning shared latent representation components from multi-institutional EHRs, in which each institution shares aggregate marginal frequencies and a low-rank spectral summary while keeping patient-level records local. items.content: Sustaining user experience (UX) quality in large-scale web search requires scalable evaluation. Traditional surveys are slow and bottleneck rapid A/B testing, while automated metrics often lack the granularity to diagnose visual-spatial UX anomalies. items.content: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatment decisions based on individual characteristics and can improve treatment outcomes beyond traditional one-size-fits-all strategies. However, similar to other commonly used algorithmic decision-making methods, ITRs without considering model fairness may result in unfair decisions across groups defined by sensitive attributes, such as race or gender. Although extensive methods have been developed for ITR estimation, most focus solely on optimizing treatment outcomes, while research on fairness-aware ITRs remains limited. items.content: Speculative decoding accelerates language-model inference by preparing candidate continuations before the target model generates them. Its efficiency depends on how well limited drafting computation anticipates the path the target will actually follow. Anticipating this path involves two sources of uncertainty: the target model's predictions and the randomness of sampling. Yet the former requires a target-model forward pass, while the latter can be fixed before drafting. items.content: Specification-guided reinforcement learning (RL) translates formal specifications of desired behavior of agents into shaped rewards. This paper introduces SLICR, a significant paradigm shift that advances the state of the art to specification-guided RL in adversarial settings under partial observability. We employ Strategy Logic (SL), which allows explicit quantification over agents' strategies and uses the linear temporal logic (LTL) to specify the agents' objectives and constraints. This enables reasoning not only about how agents should act to satisfy a specification, but also about how they should respond to the strategies and behaviors of other agents. items.summary: Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. items.content: Benchmarks for AI-based coding agents are a staple of the current AI landscape, because they are the leading way to measure the performance of LLMs. Their scores guide business and research decisions. Evaluating coding agents is challenging, since they are able to manipulate their evaluation infrastructure to artificially achieve better scores. Grading an agent's solution often requires running its code, which can then manipulate the evaluation process. BenchJack, an automated benchmark auditor, recently reached near-perfect scores on nine of ten popular agent benchmarks without actually solving their tasks. items.content: Behavioral fingerprints identify a large language model (LLM) from its responses to a shared set of prompts, enabling applications such as verifying whether a deployed model corresponds to the checkpoint it claims to be. items.content: Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. items.content: We present gauge-equivariant diffusion models as samplers for lattice gauge theories (LGTs). Using lattice gauge-equivariant convolutional neural networks (L-CNNs) and the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (MAALA), we are able to accurately sample two-dimensional U(2) field configurations and show first promising results for four-dimensional SU(3). Our two-dimensional models extrapolate remarkably well to larger inverse couplings than originally trained on. items.content: Early deep learning models attempted to simulate visual perception using a neural hierarchy that alternated between two types of layer: one modelled on cortical simple cells (that was designed to increase selectivity), and one modelled on cortical complex cells (that aimed to increase tolerance). We show that such a neural network (NN) architecture, when implemented with novel components that are better able to learn selective and tolerant representations, is capable of accurate and robust image classification and improved alignment between the behaviour of the model and the perceptual abilities of humans. Firstly, the proposed models are shallow, fewer than ten layer-pairs, which is more consistent with the rapid feedforward object categorisation performed by the biological visual system.

items.content: We present ChildAI-Gov, an explainable AI system for assessing whether education-technology (EdTech) policies respect children's digital rights. Generative AI is reaching children's education faster than its governance can keep pace, yet checking a tool against children's rights remains manual, expert-dependent, and slow. We propose the Child Rights Impact Score (CRIS), an evidence-linked measure across five dimensions: safety, privacy, transparency, autonomy, and non-discrimination. ChildAI-Gov reads an EdTech tool's privacy or AI policy and scores each dimension by combining a large-language-model judgement (gpt-4o-mini) with a deterministic rule check. items.summary: Segmenting organelles in electron microscopy (EM) volumes requires dense annotations that take experts months to produce, and every gain in imaging resolution adds to this cost. items.content: Segmenting organelles in electron microscopy (EM) volumes requires dense annotations that take experts months to produce, and every gain in imaging resolution adds to this cost. Sparsely supervised methods reduce this cost to a small fraction of labeled pixels, but the convolutional networks they build on see a limited neighborhood around each pixel, while the identity of an organelle often depends on context far beyond it. items.content: Voice cloning now needs only seconds of audio, and detectors tuned to one dataset often fail when the generator, channel, or language changes. We introduce ARCAS 290M, Neural Defend's foundation model for detecting AI-generated audio. A single frozen production model, with no benchmark-specific fine-tuning, generalizes across text-to-speech, voice-conversion, and codec-language-model generators, telephone and Bluetooth channels, recording conditions, and languages. We evaluate it on the complete official test sets of ten public benchmarks, scoring every recording exactly as released, and against commercial systems on independent leaderboards. items.content: Current decoder large language models rely on a combination of attention, feed forward and residual layers. The attention used is autoregressive (AR) though this is not strictly correct, as we note. That motivates the introduction of other attention methods that, while also not strictly AR, do enhance the AR character. One is based on a decomposition of mutual information (MI) into a set of Conditional MIs (CMIs) that correlate key tokens with pairs of query tokens. A second, higher-order attention, introduces correlations between contiguous key and query tokens. items.summary: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable significant progress in scientific tasks. items.content: Recent advancements in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable significant progress in scientific tasks. However, these models are generally assumed to be presented with complete and accurate information, overlooking the challenges of erroneous/missing information in wild scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Scientific Model Robustness, which defines a model's ability to detect anomalies, assess solvability, and perform self-calibration when faced with Information Error (inconsistencies) or Information Loss (insufficiency). Specifically, we present RoSci-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark of 1,220 samples using a seed-variant strategy across six degradation types. items.content: Scientific discourse depends on argumentative reasoning: identifying claims, evaluating evidence, and constructing coherent responses. items.content: Decision models receive a question with a closed list of answers and return a probability for each answer instead of free text. They promise low latency and robustness to prompt wording, but no study has compared several of them with fine-tuned encoders across languages. items.content: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. items.content: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. items.content: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. items.title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
items.summary: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-fra
items.content: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. items.summary: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. items.content: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor's error. items.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. items.content: A passing UVM regression shows the design agrees with the reference model on what the scoreboard checks, not that it meets the specification. Bugs that pass every test yet violate the specification, termed scoreboard escapes, survive mature testbenches. We present Verify the Verifier, to our knowledge the first framework whose LLM-based Anomaly Cross-Checker examines a passing regression's traces against the specification. Of 564 bugs inserted into four OpenTitan IPs, 68 are candidate scoreboard escapes: non-equivalent, exercised by the tests, yet passing. items.content: Graphic designs are ordered compositions of RGBA layers whose separation enables selection, movement, and reuse. Existing layered models represent each layer with a full-canvas or region-sized spatial latent grid, so representation size grows with the cumulative spatial extent of the layers. We present ProtoDiffusion, a latent-diffusion framework built on ProtoVAE, a multi-layer variational autoencoder that encodes a design into one shared spatial prototype and one candidate vector per layer. Each candidate conditions a shared decoder to reconstruct its corresponding RGBA layer. For $N$ layers, the representation contains $HW+N$ tokens before backbone-specific packing, compared with $NHW$ for full-grid-per-layer representations. items.content: Large Web platforms operate large fleets of ranking models, each selecting features from a shared pool of tens of thousands. We present an end-to-end agentic system that optimizes features across the fleet under resource constraints shared across models and those set per model, such as feature pipeline cost and serving throughput (QPS), respectively. items.content: Attention in large language models (LLMs) scores every query against every key with a full dot product. We investigate whether this dot product must be computed completely for attention to be effective. We propose Hidden Sparse Attention (HiSA), which keeps the query and key projections intact but only computes a partial dot product, following a static, parameter-free rule set by the token positions: attention becomes sparse in the hidden (feature) dimension, an axis much less explored than token sparsity, rather than over tokens as in almost all sparse attention methods. Based on the structure of rotary position embeddings (RoPE), we decompose keys and queries into parts which can be omitted when computing attention. items.title: One Framework to Diagnose Them All: A Stratified Benchmark for Bengali LLM Hallucination
items.summary: Hallucination research in low-resource languages fragments easily: each newly named failure mode prompts its own dataset, spending scarce annotators on incomparable resources. We argue for consolidation and test it at community scale. Alikbachan is a Bengali hallucination-detection benchmark stratif
items.content: Hallucination research in low-resource languages fragments easily: each newly named failure mode prompts its own dataset, spending scarce annotators on incomparable resources. We argue for consolidation and test it at community scale. Alikbachan is a Bengali hallucination-detection benchmark stratified along three crossed axes: a human-validated cultural-distance band, six task types, and a five-family, 32-mode hallucination taxonomy. It comprises a harvested 2,516-item test set (Phase 1) and a quota-constructed, gold-labeled 5,000-item set (Phase 2). The stratification is diagnostic. Four zero-shot LLM judges vary by over 30 macro-F1 points across strata, and the item-level predictions of 99 Phase-1 and 32 Phase-2 competition systems reproduce the profile: discourse-level omission defeats

items.content: Target Language Extraction (TLE) aims to isolate speech in a target language from multilingual mixtures. items.content: Peer review relies on several readers finding different problems. We measure critique overlap in conference and journal reviews. At ICLR, measured overlap rose from 12.0% in 2026 to 21.3% in 2027, in reviews from the same stage of the review process, with year-on-year rises at NeurIPS, ICML and the F1000 and PLOS journals. items.content: Thinking with images (TwI) empowers vision-language models (VLMs) to overcome perceptual bottlenecks by actively cropping and zooming into fine-grained visual details, promising both higher accuracy and interpretable, region-grounded reasoning. items.summary: World models can imagine how a physical scene evolves over the next few seconds, but growers need to know how a crop will develop over weeks to months: will this rice plant have headed a month from now, and how will it look at harvest? items.content: World models can imagine how a physical scene evolves over the next few seconds, but growers need to know how a crop will develop over weeks to months: will this rice plant have headed a month from now, and how will it look at harvest? We introduce agricultural world modeling, the task of predicting how the same plant will look at a requested horizon of days to months, from one photo of it, its cultivar, and its camera view. In preliminary analysis, even state-of-the-art image generators get this wrong: they often grow the plant too little or give it the color and form of the wrong growth stage. items.title: RL Can Only Reinforce What It Sees Succeed
items.summary: When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games played by
items.content: When a familiar rule stops working, an agent has to weigh what pre-training taught it against what it now observes. We ask how outcome-reward reinforcement learning (RL) changes this balance, in a puzzle world where both sides are known: small language models trained from scratch on games played by a Bayesian player, so that the prior and the right answer are exact. Base models hedge as their corpus did, and RL turns that hedging into decisions, in whichever direction the reward favours. But RL can only reinforce what it sees succeed. When the right action is rare, each run either learns it everywhere or not at all, and which runs take off is predicted before training by one count: the expected number of groups of attempts in which the action wins. About 35 such groups give even odds. The

items.title: Understanding MoE Decisions Beyond Gradients
items.summary: Understanding a language model's decision requires knowing how its internal computations affect its preference between answers. Gradient-based methods estimate this influence by predicting the effect of changing those computations. In mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, replacing one expert can change
items.content: Understanding a language model's decision requires knowing how its internal computations affect its preference between answers. Gradient-based methods estimate this influence by predicting the effect of changing those computations. In mixture-of-experts (MoE) models, replacing one expert can change which experts later layers select. Those switches can alter the answer scores in ways that derivatives do not capture. We introduce a predictor that uses the model's own expert outputs and selection rules to estimate these extra effects, then adds them to a second-order prediction. Across questions from three benchmarks, our method reduces the error in predicting answer-score changes by 60\% on Qwen3.6 and 47\% on Gemma4, relative to a multistep baseline using gradients and second derivatives.

items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are a
items.content: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. items.content: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation. In our setup, it uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier. items.content: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. items.title: Who are you? The Personal Imitation Game
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establ
items.content: Large Language Models (LLMs) now perform strongly on Alan Turing's 1950 Imitation Game, so we propose a harder challenge, the Personal Imitation Game, which asks whether a machine can replicate a specific individual in conversation rather than a generic human. Testing with 30 participants, we establish a human baseline and report the identity signals interrogators rely on: stylometric features, personality traits, and biographical facts. To demonstrate the framework, we design an LLM-based system that plays the game for one of the paper's authors, drawing on an autoethnographic dataset spanning ten years of personal digital communication. items.content: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. items.content: One popular architecture for multi-agent systems (MAS) relies on an orchestrator that generates an initial plan, coordinates its execution, and dynamically revises the plan based on agent feedback when tasks cannot be fully specified in advance. items.content: Self-supervised video encoders are commonly trained to either reconstruct pixels or predict latent features, yet it remains unclear how these objectives shape representations for downstream dynamics. We present a capacity-matched study isolating this choice: two identical video encoders with a shared FSQ bottleneck are trained under autoencoding and V-JEPA objectives on a continuous control environment. We introduce a simple asymmetric discretization scheme to apply the same bottleneck to the predictive model. The resulting representations exhibit a clear trade-off: the autoencoder preserves substantially more physical state information and achieves slightly better one-step latent prediction, while the predictive encoder accumulates less error under autoregressive rollout. items.content: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. items.content: Deployed world-action models (WAMs) can keep improving only if they make good use of their own experience. Existing methods supply retrieved rollouts or demonstrations to the policy as context, yet such experience often turns previously solved tasks into failures. What, then, makes good experience for a WAM? We show that experience is valuable only in use: its value depends not on whether the source rollout succeeded but on what is stored, when it is used, and where it enters the policy. We therefore propose F$^3$, which makes these three decisions with Form, Fit, and Fusion. items.content: We introduce Clover-35B-A3B-Preview (Clover), a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model with 35 billion total parameters and 3 billion activated parameters, supporting thinking-mode generation. Clover adapts Gated Delta Networks to block diffusion by combining recurrent memory of previously generated context with bidirectional softmax attention inside the current block. Historical memory readout competes with current-block tokens in a shared softmax, with learnable block-size calibration and a separate, zero-initialized right-context convolution branch. Clover leads the seven evaluated agent metrics, including 73.6 on SWE-bench Verified and 51.7 on Terminal-Bench 2.1. items.content: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting improves the performance of Large Language Models by eliciting intermediate reasoning steps. However, CoT is far from perfect: on some tasks, models perform worse than with direct-answer prompting, and on others they generate a few hundred tokens to reach the correct answer. A linear probe shows that the model encodes these two classes differently. items.title: Late Entry in Looped Language Models
items.summary: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-va
items.content: Looped language models deepen reasoning at a compact parameter count by iterating a shared layer stack T times per token, turning recurrence depth directly into sequential decoding latency. Conventional early-exit decoding halts after initial passes without cache completion, truncating cached key-value states of past tokens to shallow depth. We study the opposite strategy, late entry, where new tokens skip initial passes and enter directly into the final K < T passes over a deep context cache. Once lightweight fine-tuning resolves hidden-state norm mismatch at the entry boundary, deep cached context substitutes for skipped token-local passes, allowing late entry to outperform matched early exit across model families and pass budgets. items.summary: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extend a Transformer's residual stream into multiple parallel streams with learned cross-stream connections. items.content: Manifold-constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) extend a Transformer's residual stream into multiple parallel streams with learned cross-stream connections. Prior work trains all streams toward a shared objective. items.summary: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and
items.content: Building a small language model requires choosing which published improvements to combine. We compare five changes in the same model, using the same data and training budget. We test selected combinations and repeat each one with a second random seed. Mixture-of-experts layers, Muon optimisation and a Gated DeltaNet hybrid give the largest gains. Extra normalisation also helps, while an attention gate with a matched parameter budget adds little on average. The gains mostly combine, but small interactions between changes appear again in the repeated runs. Repetition also reveals benefits that an initial statistical estimate treated as noise. items.content: Patient history taking is a strategic, multi-turn process that refines diagnostic hypotheses through iterative questioning, mirroring clinical reasoning where each inquiry updates beliefs over candidate diagnoses. items.summary: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. items.content: Multimodal Entity Linking (MEL) aims to disambiguate mentions in multimodal contexts by grounding them to specific entities in a knowledge base. A pivotal challenge in MEL is capturing multi-level correspondences: the semantic consistency between mention-entity pairs and the complementary correlations across modalities. In response, we propose the Multi-Element Collaborative Interaction (MECI) framework. items.title: Why Modern LLMs Don’t Look Like the Original Transformer
items.summary: Author(s): Saurabh Singh Originally published on Towards AI. Why Modern LLMs Don’t Look Like the Original Transformer The familiar diagram had two halves. Follow what changed when the job grew beyond translation. If you’ve ever tried to understand an LLM, you’ve probably come across this picture. It
items.content: Author(s): Saurabh Singh Originally published on Towards AI. Why Modern LLMs Don’t Look Like the Original Transformer The familiar diagram had two halves. Follow what changed when the job grew beyond translation. If you’ve ever tried to understand an LLM, you’ve probably come across this picture. It is Figure 1 from Attention Is All You Need, the 2017 paper that introduced the Transformer. There is a lot going on: colored boxes, looping arrows, and two tall stacks that seem to do slightly different versions of the same thing. It is easier to follow once you give the machine a sentence to work on. Suppose we want to translate “The cat is sleeping” into German. The left stack reads the English sentence. The right stack writes “Die Katze schläft.” Now look inside a model such as Llama 3.1. That separate text encoder on the left is gone. One of the attention blocks on the right has gone with it. If you learned both halves because you wanted to understand chatbots, this can be confusing. The familiar drawing is still a good place to start. We just have to follow what happened after it was published. The left side was there for a reason Look at the arrow that leaves the top of the left stack and crosses into the middle attention block on the right. That connection explains why a translator needs two stacks. The encoder has read the English sentence and built a representation of each token. The decoder can consult those representations while deciding which German token to produce next. When it has written “Die Katze,” it still has access to the English words “is sleeping.” It can use that source information alongside the German text it has already produced. This is the role of cross-attention, the attention between the two stacks. The bottom attention block on the right has another job. It looks at the output written so far. Its mask prevents a position from seeing later output tokens, which would give away the answer during training. So the decoder was already a machine for writing one token after another. The encoder gave it a separate piece of text to consult. That translation story is also where I start in The Translator That Forgot, my visual walkthrough of the paper. Following a sentence through the model makes the arrows much easier to understand than starting with the names of every box. It also makes the next change easier to see. What changed when the model learned to keep writing A translator learns from pairs of texts. Here is the English sentence; here is its German translation. But there is much more ordinary text available than neatly paired examples. Books, webpages and code all contain a different kind of training example: a passage followed by whatever comes next. A model can read a prefix, predict the next token, and learn from whether it was right. Do that across a large corpus, and the same task exposes it to grammar, facts, writing styles and patterns in code. The first GPT paper used a Transformer decoder for this kind of generative pretraining in 2018. Now there is no separate source sentence to encode. The earlier text is already in the same sequence as the text being predicted. A causal attention stack can process that prefix directly. This is the important difference between a decoder-only model and simply covering up the left side of the old picture. The cross-attention block that used to read the encoder’s output goes away too. A chat application can then arrange a conversation as one sequence, using markers to identify the user, assistant and other parts of the exchange. The model continues that sequence with the assistant’s response. Instruction tuning and other post-training help turn a text continuation model into something that follows requests. During training, the text is already available, so the model can process many positions together while masking future tokens. When it generates a new answer, the ordinary autoregressive loop still depends on the tokens it has produced so far. The old encoder has not become useless. A translation model can still use one, and a multimodal model may have a separate image encoder. Its removal from a text-only language model follows from the job that model is being trained to do. Then the conversation got expensive Once a model can continue a conversation, people naturally want it to continue a longer one. They paste a document, ask follow-up questions and expect the earlier details to remain available. For the system serving the model, those earlier tokens have a cost. Attention uses quantities called keys and values to read information from previous tokens. During generation, the system can keep these quantities in a KV cache, saving it from having to recompute them every time it writes another token. Each attention layer keeps its own cache. As the sequence grows, more cached numbers accumulate. Consider an illustrative model with 32 layers, 32 query heads and 128 numbers per head. Suppose it has 8,192 tokens in context and stores each cached number in two bytes. If every query head has its own key and value head, the cache payload is 4 GiB for that one sequence. The model’s weights and other runtime memory are extra. That is a substantial bill for remembering what has already been said. Grouped-query attention, or GQA, changes how that work is shared. Several query heads use the same key and value head. The queries still differ, but the model learns to work with shared keys and values. With eight KV heads instead of 32, the same calculation gives 1 GiB. The arithmetic for the eight-head case is: 2 × 32 layers × 8,192 tokens × 8 KV heads × 128 numbers × 2 bytes = 1,073,741,824 bytes, or 1 GiB. The first 2 counts keys and values. Keep all the other assumptions fixed and multiply the KV heads by four, and you get the 4 GiB case. This saving applies […]

items.title: Microsoft’s Qubit Now Lasts 20 Seconds. The Hard Question Is Still Open.
items.summary: Author(s): Siddhant Nitin Patil Originally published on Towards AI. Microsoft’s Qubit Now Lasts 20 Seconds. The Hard Question Is Still Open. Photo by Brecht Corbeel on Unsplash A thousand times better, from a few small changes Microsoft’s Majorana 2 video makes a striking pitch. After 20 years of wo
items.content: Author(s): Siddhant Nitin Patil Originally published on Towards AI. Microsoft’s Qubit Now Lasts 20 Seconds. The Hard Question Is Still Open. Photo by Brecht Corbeel on Unsplash A thousand times better, from a few small changes Microsoft’s Majorana 2 video makes a striking pitch. After 20 years of work on topological quantum computing, the team says it went from Majorana 1 to Majorana 2 in about a year and saw a thousandfold improvement in stability. The changes were in the materials. Majorana 1 used aluminum as its superconductor. Majorana 2 uses lead, and the semiconductor stack now adds antimony to the indium arsenide, grown on a gallium antimonide substrate. In Microsoft’s technical paper, released at Build on June 2, the measured parity lifetime rose from roughly 1 to 12 milliseconds in the aluminum devices to about 22 seconds in the lead device, with some intervals lasting over a minute. The video explains why that matters with simple arithmetic. If an operation takes a microsecond and the qubit’s state lasts a millisecond, you get about one error every thousand operations. If it lasts 20 seconds, you can run tens of millions of operations before a flip. And because that lifetime depends exponentially on the energy gap, modest gains add up fast: the topological gap went from about 30 to about 70 microelectronvolts, and the lifetime went up by more than three orders of magnitude. Microsoft also pulled its target forward. It now expects a scalable, commercially useful quantum computer by 2029, which it says halves its previous timeline. Postquantum’s analysis puts the earlier target at 2033. The consensus: topological quantum computing has arrived If you only watch the video, the story is simple. Theory became reality. Lead was the moment the team saw that what it had predicted actually works. A qubit whose state holds for seconds instead of milliseconds is far more robust, and a machine built from those qubits could reach the chemistry and materials problems no classical computer can solve exactly. The video goes further. Microsoft pitches a loop between quantum and AI: quantum computers produce exact answers about molecules and materials, AI models learn from them, and eventually a Copilot could design materials as easily as it writes an essay. Microsoft also says it used its Microsoft Discovery agentic AI tools to speed up fabrication and measurement, including an agent that found an uncalibrated temperature sensor skewing fabrication data. And there is outside momentum. Microsoft is one of two companies, alongside PsiQuantum, in the final stage of DARPA’s US2QC program, part of its Quantum Benchmarking Initiative. The video addresses skeptics directly. A researcher in it says skepticism is a healthy part of science and that people who look carefully at the results find them “quite revolutionary.” That is where the story needs a closer look. Breaking it: a better material is not yet a proven qubit Read the paper and the outside analysis, and the picture splits in two. What Majorana 2 shows is solid materials progress, per Microsoft’s paper as summarized by Postquantum and The Quantum Insider: A parity lifetime of about 22 seconds, measured over 324 intervals in one wire of one tetron. A parent superconducting gap of about 1,300 microelectronvolts with lead, against about 300 with aluminum. A topological gap of about 70 microelectronvolts, against about 30 before. A new radio-frequency method that resolves low-energy states to about 1 microelectronvolt. Source: Microsoft’s June 2, 2026 paper, as summarized by Microsoft and Postquantum. Values approximate; lifetime measured in one wire of one device; not peer reviewed. Chart by the author. What it does not show yet: X-basis measurements. The paper reports only Z-parity data. A qubit needs both. Critics argue that a long Z lifetime alone can also come from topologically trivial states. Qubit operations. No gates, entanglement or algorithms are in the paper. Nayak told Science that control and algorithm data exist but are unpublished. The full unit cell. Measurements are on a single wire, not the four-tetron prototype. Independent review. The Quantum Insider notes the paper was not peer reviewed, and there is no data across multiple identical devices. The history matters here. When Microsoft announced Majorana 1 in February 2025, Nature’s editorial note on the accompanying paper said the results did not represent evidence of Majorana zero modes. This June, Nature published a critique by St Andrews physicist Henry Legg arguing that the plotting code behind Microsoft’s 2025 topological gap results showed only the largest passing region and left others out. Microsoft called it a minor off-by-one-pixel bug, and Chetan Nayak said: “We stand by our results and our roadmap.” So the same lifetime number reads two ways. To Microsoft, it is protected quantum information. To critics like Legg and Pittsburgh’s Sergey Frolov, the question of whether those states are topological at all has not been answered. The truth: everyone now says 2029, and DARPA will grade it Step back and Microsoft’s date stops looking unusual. IBM has said since June 2025 that it will build Starling, a fault-tolerant machine with about 200 logical qubits, by 2029. Quantinuum, which raised about $1.7 billion in its June IPO, has an Apollo system on its roadmap for 2029. Google, which has not named a year, showed in October that magic state cultivation on Willow cut errors about 40-fold, a step toward fault tolerance. 2029 has become the industry’s default answer. What separates these bets is not the date. It is the kind of evidence behind it. IBM, Google and Quantinuum are scaling qubits that everyone agrees are qubits, and arguing about error rates. Microsoft is betting on a qubit whose basic nature is still disputed, in exchange for a potentially much bigger payoff: if topological protection is real, it could need far less error-correction overhead per useful qubit. That is why the most important development since the launch is not in the video. In September, Microsoft opened a 15,000-square-foot quantum center at the University of Maryland with a room where DARPA can boot […]

items.title: Does Smarter Tuning Pay Off? Confopt vs Optuna’s Default on 131 Datasets
items.summary: Author(s): Ilia Ekhlakov Originally published on Towards AI. Does Smarter Tuning Pay Off? Confopt vs Optuna’s Default on 131 Datasets Assumes you have tuned a model with Optuna. The first draft of this article said that ConfOpt and TPE tie. ConfOpt is a hyperparameter sampler that accounts for noise
items.content: Author(s): Ilia Ekhlakov Originally published on Towards AI. Does Smarter Tuning Pay Off? Confopt vs Optuna’s Default on 131 Datasets Assumes you have tuned a model with Optuna. The first draft of this article said that ConfOpt and TPE tie. ConfOpt is a hyperparameter sampler that accounts for noise in the scores it sees, and TPE, the tree-structured Parzen estimator, is Optuna’s default. I had two sampler seeds of each, a gap of +0.0011 PR AUC (area under the precision-recall curve) and a 95% interval that included zero, and I read that as a tie. Then I added three more seeds. Over five seeds the gap is +0.0016, its interval excludes zero, and ConfOpt is ahead on four seeds of five. The data never said tie. It said that two seeds could not tell. The whole study is about noise. A hyperparameter search maximizes a number, and that number is a measurement. It changes when the seed changes, and the best of many such measurements is biased upward. Previously I measured this bias, and its size surprised me: on 8 large datasets, a 200-trial TPE search reported a gain of 2.75 accuracy points over its first trial, and the same winners gained 0.99 on rows the search never saw (run-noise notebook). If the score is a noisy reading, a search that accounts for the noise should choose better than a search that trusts every reading. That is the argument for ConfOpt. Its sampler, the part of a search that proposes the next configuration, fits quantile regression to the trial history. It then calibrates the result with conformal prediction, a way to give prediction intervals a stated coverage. ConfOpt’s OptunaHub page says its single-fidelity performance “in popular HPO benchmarks puts it consistently ahead of TPE and SMAC” (HPO is hyperparameter optimization; single-fidelity means every trial trains the full model). I wanted to check that claim on small data, where the noise is largest, so I put ConfOpt in place of TPE in the tuning of my small-data benchmark. The short version: LightGBM, 131 datasets, 50 trials per search, five sampler seeds each. ConfOpt scored 0.0016 PR AUC above TPE on average, with a 95% interval of [+0.0006, +0.0027]. The gap is a mean, not a typical dataset: the median is zero, and five small datasets carry two thirds of it. When the search selected on PR AUC, ConfOpt also produced worse-calibrated models, with an expected calibration error (ECE, the gap between predicted confidence and actual accuracy) of 0.077 against 0.068. Its search took about 1.8 times as long. I keep TPE as my default for now, and the last section says why. One caveat comes first: I did not tune ConfOpt the way its authors would, and I added the extra seeds and several controls after I saw the first results. Read the numbers as a test of the defaults of ConfOpt’s OptunaHub wrapper, the module that plugs ConfOpt into Optuna. A search maximizes a number that is partly luck Two kinds of noise sit in the score that a search maximizes. The first is the seed: train the same model on the same rows with another seed, and the score changes. The second is selection bias: the best of many noisy scores is ahead of its true level, because the search picked it for being high. I measured both in October on real data. Across 40 seeds of CatBoost with default parameters, accuracy on 1,000 test rows had a standard deviation of 0.29 points (median over 9 large OpenML datasets). Selection bias was larger. After 200 TPE trials, each scored on 1,000 rows, most of the gain that the search reported did not reach 20,000 held-out rows (Figure 1). Figure 1. The gain a TPE search reports, and the gain on rows it never saw. The trial axis is not linear. Samplers that account for noise Optuna’s default sampler, TPE, has no noise setting: its constructor takes none (checked in Optuna 4.7.0). It ranks trials by the score it observed. Other samplers deal with noise in two ways. Gaussian-process samplers treat it as a variance, which they learn from the data (Optuna’s GPSampler, BoTorch’s SingleTaskGP) or take from you (OptunaHub’s heteroscedastic_gp). SMAC3 averages the noise out by repeating evaluations over several seeds. ConfOpt does neither: it does not estimate the noise of a metric as a separate quantity. It predicts quantiles of the scores it has seen and calibrates those intervals, so the noise appears as interval width. The ConfOpt paper argues that Gaussian processes struggle with categorical hyperparameters and with data that is skewed or has non-constant variance. The method builds on a 2023 ICML paper by Salinas and colleagues, which notes that a Gaussian process makes “strong assumptions about the observation noise, which might not be warranted in practice”. I tested only ConfOpt, because its page makes a direct claim about TPE. What ConfOpt’s OptunaHub wrapper does by default My test was cheap to set up: through OptunaHub only the sampler changes, and the search space, the budget, the folds and the objective stay the same as for TPE. The swap looks like this: import optunaimport optunahub# shortened: the real space has nine LightGBM parametersspace = { "learning_rate": optuna.distributions.FloatDistribution(1e-3, 0.3, log=True), "n_estimators": optuna.distributions.IntDistribution(50, 500), "class_weight": optuna.distributions.CategoricalDistribution(["balanced", "none"]),}module = optunahub.load_module("samplers/confopt_sampler", ref="180d82259844f17578f4c3d0f8472835c17ff8cb")sampler = module.ConfOptSampler(search_space=space, seed=0)study = optuna.create_study(direction="maximize", sampler=sampler)study.optimize(objective, n_trials=50) # your objective, with matching trial.suggest_* calls Unlike TPE, ConfOpt needs the search space up front, as a dict of Optuna distributions. The objective keeps its usual trial.suggest_* calls. The wrapper is not ConfOpt as its authors would run it. I read its code at registry commit 180d822, for confopt 2.0.1. The defaults are: a quantile gradient boosting surrogate (searcher="qgbm"); optimistic Bayesian sampling as the acquisition function; 3,000 random candidates scored per trial; 10 random opening trials; conformal calibration only when more than 32 trials are finished (n_pre_conformal_trials=32). The last default matters at my budget of 50 trials. The first 10 trials are random, the next 23 are guided by […]

items.title: Unified Radix Cache Explained: One Tree for Full Attention, Sliding Window and Mamba
items.summary: Author(s): Aadishagrawal Originally published on Towards AI. Unified Radix Cache Explained: One Tree for Full Attention, Sliding Window and Mamba A walkthrough of how SGLang caches prefixes for hybrid LLMs. If you serve LLMs, you already know the cheapest token is the one you never recompute. Prefix
items.content: Author(s): Aadishagrawal Originally published on Towards AI. Unified Radix Cache Explained: One Tree for Full Attention, Sliding Window and Mamba A walkthrough of how SGLang caches prefixes for hybrid LLMs. If you serve LLMs, you already know the cheapest token is the one you never recompute. Prefix caching makes that possible: when two requests start with the same text, the second one reuses the work done for the first. That trick is easy for classic transformers. It gets tricky for hybrid models that mix different kinds of layers. SGLang’s answer is the Unified Radix Cache (URC), introduced by the LMSYS team in August 2026. This post explains the problem, the design, and how it behaves in practice, using small examples you can follow by hand. What you’ll learn Why one cache rule no longer fits all models What full attention, sliding window attention (SWA) and Mamba each need to remember How URC uses one tree with pluggable components How HiCache spreads that cache across GPU, CPU and external storage How a prefix is accepted or rejected, with examples How session-aware eviction beats plain LRU An end-to-end example that ties everything together A note on the numbers. Token counts in the examples are small round numbers I chose for readability. The rules and the benchmark results come from the LMSYS announcement and the SGLang docs. I haven’t verified every internal detail against the source code, and I flag the spots where I’m inferring. 1. Background: why a unified tree is needed Prefix caching in one minute When an LLM processes a prompt, it computes a KV cache: key/value tensors for every token that later tokens attend to. If a new request begins with the same tokens as an earlier one (a system prompt, a chat history, a code repository), those tensors don’t need to be recomputed. SGLang tracks which prefixes are cached with a radix tree (a compressed prefix tree). Each edge is labeled with a run of tokens. To serve a new request, SGLang walks the tree, finds the longest cached prefix, and only prefills the rest. root │ [You are a helpful assistant ...] <- shared system prompt ┌────┴─────┐ [User: hi ...] [User: fix my bug ...] <- two different conversations For a plain full-attention transformer this works perfectly, because cached KV for a prefix stays valid no matter what is appended later. Where it breaks: hybrid models Many recent models mix layer types in one network. A request now carries several kinds of cached state, and each has its own notion of “reusable”: Full attention KV is reusable across the whole matched prefix. Sliding window attention KV only covers the trailing window. A recurrent (Mamba-style) state is valid only at an exact checkpoint. All three share the same token prefix, but not the same reusable boundary. If you force one boundary on all of them, you either throw away valid reuse or, worse, allow invalid reuse and get wrong outputs. The old approach: a class for every combination Early on, SGLang handled this with separate cache classes, such as RadixCache, MambaRadixCache and SWARadixCache. Each re-implemented matching, insertion, locking and eviction. Add an orthogonal feature like HiCache (hierarchical caching) and the number of combinations multiplies. Full only + SWA + Mamba + all three no HiCache Cache A Cache B Cache C Cache D + HiCache Cache E Cache F Cache G Cache H <- the "class matrix" URC replaces this matrix with one tree and pluggable components. A new model family picks a combination instead of requiring a new tree. 2. Three kinds of memory, in plain words Before looking at the design, here is what each layer type actually needs to remember, and why. Full attention: remember every past token In full attention, each new token looks back at all earlier tokens. So the cache holds a key/value pair for every token so far, and it grows linearly with context length. Because attention is causal (a token only depends on tokens before it), the KV for tokens 1..N stays correct no matter what comes next. That is why any prefix length is a valid reuse point. Sliding window attention (SWA): remember only the recent tail In sliding window attention, each token only looks at the last W tokens. Older keys and values will never be read again by these layers, so only a trailing window is kept. To resume from position p, you need the KV for tokens p-W+1 … p, and they must be contiguous. Memory is bounded by W instead of growing with the sequence. Mamba (recurrent state): remember one checkpoint Recurrent layers don’t store per-token keys and values. They fold the entire history into one fixed-size state, updated token by token. That makes memory constant regardless of length. The catch: the state at position 550 is a blend of all 550 tokens. You can’t “subtract” tokens to get the state at position 300. So a Mamba state is only reusable at the exact position where it was saved. That position is called a checkpoint. Side by side Hybrid models combine these. According to the LMSYS post, DeepSeek-V4 uses full attention plus SWA, Kimi-K3 uses full attention plus a recurrent (KDA) state, and Inkling uses all three. 3. What is the Unified Radix Cache? URC is built on one separation of concerns: Prefix identity (which tokens is this?) lives in one shared radix tree. Reuse validity (is the cached data usable here?) lives in components that attach to tree nodes. Here is the picture. One tree, three kinds of attached data: one token-keyed radix tree (the shared topology) root ──► n1 ──► n2 ──► n3 ──► n4 │ │ │ │ FULL ● ● ● ● KV for every token on the path SWA ○ ○ ○ ● trailing window only (○ = tombstone) MAMBA ○ ○ ○ ● checkpoint only where saved (○ = none) ● = data present ○ = empty slot, node still in the tree Each tree node stores references […]

items.title: Your Dashboard Says “200 OK,” but Your AI Agent Gave the Wrong Answer. Now What?
items.summary: Author(s): Ashwini T Originally published on Towards AI. Your Dashboard Says “200 OK,” but Your AI Agent Gave the Wrong Answer. Now What? A user tells you the answer was wrong. You rush to your monitoring dashboard. Everything is green. Requests are succeeding, error rates are flat, and response tim
items.content: Author(s): Ashwini T Originally published on Towards AI. Your Dashboard Says “200 OK,” but Your AI Agent Gave the Wrong Answer. Now What? A user tells you the answer was wrong. You rush to your monitoring dashboard. Everything is green. Requests are succeeding, error rates are flat, and response times look healthy. Your CEO agent shows a calm “200 OK” in 2.3 seconds. And yet, somewhere inside that smooth-looking request, something went wrong. You just can’t see where. If that feeling sounds familiar, or if you want to avoid it, this post is for you. We’ll look at why traditional monitoring misses the problems in multi-agent systems, and how a tool called MLflow can give you real visibility into what your agents are doing, using a mortgage lending example to keep it concrete. Why “200 OK” isn’t enough Traditional monitoring was built for a world where a request either works or breaks, and where the same input gives the same output. It checks HTTP status codes, error rates, and speed. Multi-agent AI doesn’t behave that way. A request can return perfectly “successfully” while the agent inside it did something quietly wrong. Your dashboard says the request happened. It doesn’t say whether the agent picked the right tool, whether a data source came back empty, or whether you burned tokens on a prompt nobody has reviewed in months. So we need something deeper, often called LLM observability. The idea is simple: record what happened at every step, not just whether the request finished. Our example: a mortgage lending assistant Imagine you’ve built an app where people chat about their needs, and the system tells them which loans they might qualify for. Under the hood, a FastAPI service routes each request to one of five agents, each with its own persona: A prospector A borrower agent A loan officer An underwriter A CEO assistant for internal analytics These agents call tools like databases, language models, and MCP servers, and all of that happens before the user sees a reply. That’s a lot of moving parts, and a lot of places for things to hide. Four failures your dashboard can’t see 1. Silent tool failures. An MCP tool returns empty data, and the agent carries on anyway, confidently answering from incomplete information. In a lending context, that’s the kind of mistake that makes your stomach drop. 2. Cascading latency. A slow database query delays a model call, which delays the whole response. From the outside, you only know it was slow. You can’t tell which link in the chain was the culprit. 3. Context overflow. An agent stuffs too much into a prompt, the call fails with a cryptic error, and the user sees a generic timeout. 4. Nondeterminism. Ask the same question twice and you may get different results, so the bug often refuses to reproduce on your laptop. That also means you have no quality baseline, no proof that your agents are consistent and accurate. In a regulated field like lending, that isn’t just annoying. It can become a compliance problem. Seeing this list made me feel two things at once: worry, because these are so easy to miss, and relief, because each one has a practical answer. The answer: traces and spans MLflow’s core idea is the trace, a complete record of one request. A trace is made of spans. Each span is one step, such as a single model call, a tool use, or a database query. Spans are organized as a parent-and-child tree, so you can see what called what, with which inputs and outputs, and how long each step took. MLflow Tracing captures inputs, outputs, and metadata for each intermediate step of a request, which helps you pinpoint the source of bugs and unexpected behavior. Along the way, you also get token counts, per-step latency, tool parameters, prompt-and-response pairs, and database results. You can tag traces with user and session IDs too. That means when a customer says, “the answer was wrong,” you can pull up their session and replay the agent’s decision path, step by step. Instead of guessing, you’re reading the story of what happened. It also helps before production. In a notebook, you can tweak prompts and run evaluations with fast feedback, long before real users touch the system. Grading your agents with “LLM judges” Some checks are simple and deterministic: a regex match, an exact match, a latency limit. But what about quality? “Was this answer helpful?” doesn’t fit neatly into a regex. That’s where LLM-as-a-judge comes in. You use a second model to grade your agent’s output against criteria you define. The video suggests judging things like: Tool call correctness: did the agent choose the right tools? Call efficiency: did it get there in few steps, or wander? Relevance: did the answer address what the user asked? Safety: is the response appropriate? Guidelines: your own rules, written in plain language. For the mortgage assistant, that might be “Be helpful, never promise a rate, keep it professional.” That last one is my favorite, because it turns compliance rules into something testable. MLflow’s Guidelines scorer takes criteria you write yourself, such as “the answer must be concise and straight to the point.” A small example, based on MLflow’s documented pattern: import mlflowfrom mlflow.genai.scorers import RelevanceToQuery, Guidelines results = mlflow.genai.evaluate( data=eval_dataset, predict_fn=my_agent, scorers=[ RelevanceToQuery(), Guidelines( name="no_rate_promises", guidelines="Never promise a specific interest rate.", ), ],) A note of honesty: scorer availability can differ between versions and platforms. For example, the docs I found say the Safety scorer was, at one point, only available in Databricks managed MLflow. Check what your version supports before you plan around it. A prompt registry: Git for your prompts Here’s an idea that quietly saves a lot of headaches. When you find a system prompt that really works, you can register it with version control, much like you would with code. Why does that matter? A prompt change is a behavior change, and without version control you can’t connect “this […]

items.title: AI Gives You the Accelerator. But Do We Know Where We Are Going?
items.summary: Author(s): Gajanan Tayde Originally published on Towards AI. AI Gives You the Accelerator. But Do We Know Where We Are Going? Why the people who survive the AI revolution will not necessarily be the best prompt writers, but the ones who know what to build, why to build it, and how to get there. Imag
items.content: Author(s): Gajanan Tayde Originally published on Towards AI. AI Gives You the Accelerator. But Do We Know Where We Are Going? Why the people who survive the AI revolution will not necessarily be the best prompt writers, but the ones who know what to build, why to build it, and how to get there. Imagine sitting inside a car that can travel at 300 km/h. It has the most powerful engine. The latest navigation system. Advanced safety features, airbags, excellent mileage, a comfortable interior, and every technology you could possibly ask for. You press the accelerator. The car responds immediately. Within seconds, you are travelling faster than almost everyone around you. But there is one small problem. We have absolutely no idea where we are going. You take a wrong turn. But because the car is so powerful, you cover the wrong distance very quickly. You move farther and farther away from your destination. Now imagine another person walking on the road. He has no powerful engine, no advanced navigation, and no sophisticated technology. But he knows exactly where he wants to go. Who will reach the destination first? You might have the better machine. But he has something much more important: direction. This is how I see the current AI revolution. The AI revolution and the fear of being replaced Everywhere we look, there is a discussion about AI taking away jobs. People say that the work previously done by ten people can now be completed by two. Entire teams may become smaller. Tasks that required hours may take minutes. And honestly, I don’t think these concerns are completely baseless. AI can automate a tremendous amount of work. It can write code, analyse documents, generate reports, review applications, create designs, and perform tasks that once required considerable human effort. But I have a slightly different perspective. Perhaps the real question is not whether AI will replace eight people with two. The real question is: What makes those two people capable of doing the work of ten? Is it simply that they know how to write better prompts? I don’t think so. I believe those two people will be the ones who understand the problem, know what the destination looks like, possess sufficient technical knowledge to identify possible solutions, and know how to bring different capabilities together. In other words, they know how to drive. AI is the engine. Your understanding is the steering wheel. Let us return to our car. A powerful engine gives you speed. But speed alone does not guarantee progress. You need to know: Where are you going? Which road should you take? What obstacles might come along the way? When should you change your route? How do you know that you have reached the destination? Now replace the car with AI. AI gives you speed. It can generate code, suggest frameworks, explain technologies, create scripts, analyse data, and even help you build complete solutions. But who decides what needs to be built? Who understands the actual problem? Who determines whether the suggested solution is technically correct? Who knows whether the result is secure, scalable, reliable, and suitable for the intended purpose? These questions require something beyond the ability to write a prompt. They require understanding. Consider a simple example. Suppose somebody asks AI to build an application. AI may generate the code, suggest the architecture, recommend a database, and even explain how to deploy the application. But if the person asking does not understand the application’s requirements, data flow, security considerations, or architectural decisions, how will that person know whether the generated solution is actually good? The person may receive a beautifully written solution that solves the wrong problem. And because AI works so quickly, the mistake may also happen very quickly. The danger is not always that AI gives us a wrong answer. Sometimes the danger is that we do not know enough to recognise that the answer is wrong. A practical example from my own experience Let me explain this through an experience from my work in cybersecurity. When AI security testing started gaining attention, there was considerable curiosity around how we could test AI-based applications. One day, an interesting problem came up. We had to test a chatbot. Now, there was already a useful open-source security testing tool called Garak. It provides a collection of probes and techniques to assess the behaviour of language models. But there was a practical challenge. Garak was designed to interact with models through supported interfaces. Our target, however, was a chatbot application. Simply running the tool was not going to solve the problem. So, what could we do? I started thinking about the different pieces available to us. We knew that the chatbot had an API. We knew that API endpoints accepted input parameters. We also knew that Garak had its own collection of prompts and testing probes. Then came the important question: Could we connect these pieces together? What if we could make Garak generate its testing prompts, route those prompts through the chatbot’s API, capture the responses, and then collect the results? That was the direction. Instead of treating Garak and the chatbot as two completely separate things, I started looking at how their capabilities could be connected. By understanding the underlying interfaces and how the components worked, I was able to develop a script that brought these pieces together and generated a report. Now, notice something important here. The solution did not begin with a magical prompt. It began with understanding the problem. I needed to know what Garak could do, how APIs worked, how the chatbot communicated, what needed to be connected, and what the final output should look like. AI can certainly assist in writing such a script. It can help explain APIs, suggest implementation approaches, identify errors, and improve the code. But without knowing what I was trying to achieve, how would I even know what to ask? That is the difference I am trying to explain. The value […]

items.title: What Is a Model (And Why a Straight Line Already Counts As One)
items.summary: Author(s): Ramon Invarato Originally published on Towards AI. What Is a Model (And Why a Straight Line Already Counts As One) Note: Although this article can be read independently, it is part of a comprehensive interactive course — the table of contents for which can be found at https://jarroba.com/
items.content: Author(s): Ramon Invarato Originally published on Towards AI. What Is a Model (And Why a Straight Line Already Counts As One) Note: Although this article can be read independently, it is part of a comprehensive interactive course — the table of contents for which can be found at https://jarroba.com/en/ai-course/—where the entire course is available for free. “Model”, “train” and “predict” are words that come up constantly when talking about AI, and all three fit in a straight line: the model is the line, training is placing it among the points, and predicting is reading its height at a new point. Try this first Open the Regression & MLE tool. You will see ten points and a line that passes between them. The vertical gray lines joining each point to the line are the residuals: how far off the line is at that point. On the right, MSE (loss) is 0.236. MSE is the mean squared error, and loss is the name given to the error you want to make small: each error is squared, the ten are added up and the total is divided by ten. (Further down you have the calculation worked out point by point, in case you want to repeat it on paper.) Take the fifth point from the left and drag it upward. The line tilts a little toward it and the MSE goes up: the farther you move it, the more. You have not touched the line: it has recalculated itself so that the total error is the smallest possible with the new points. Look also at the equation at the top right, y = 0.687·x + 1.658: while you drag, those two numbers change. Now click Clear and click in five places on the chart to place your own points. With each click, the line repositions itself. Pay attention to the first three. With one point, the MSE is 0, but infinitely many lines pass through one point and all of them get it right; the tool picks the horizontal one. With two, the line passes exactly through both and the MSE is still 0. From the third on, if they are not aligned, no line passes through all of them and the MSE stops being 0. A line has two numbers to adjust: with two points it always gets it right, even though it has not learned anything. With three or four points, a red overfitting warning may appear. The tool runs a test: it removes one point, fits the line with the others and checks how much it misses the one it removed, and it repeats this with every point. With so few, the line clings to the ones it has and misses a lot on the one it has not seen. What makes the warning go away is adding more points: with five it usually disappears. Overfitting is covered in detail later, in Fitting a curve. What just happened You have just done all three things. The data are the points. Each one is a pair of numbers: where it is horizontally (x) and vertically (y). They could be hours of study and an exam grade, square meters and the price of an apartment, or anything that is measured in two numbers. The model is the line. A line is fixed by just two numbers: how much it tilts and at what height it crosses the vertical axis. The tool writes it at the top right; with the ten starting points it is y = 0.687·x + 1.658. Those two numbers (0.687 and 1.658) are the model: everything it has learned from the ten points fits in there. Training is searching for those two numbers. Not just any line will do: you look for the one that makes the mean of the squared errors as small as possible, the MSE you see on screen. They are squared so that an error above and another below do not cancel each other out, and so that a large error weighs much more than a small one. That is why the method is called least squares, and it is not new: Adrien-Marie Legendre published it in 1805, and in 1809 Carl Friedrich Gauss claimed that he had been using it since 1795 (Least squares, on Wikipedia). For a line, those two numbers can be calculated in one go with a formula, and that is what the tool does every time you move a point. Large models have so many numbers that no formula gets them all at once, and they are adjusted in small steps, correcting a little on each pass (that way of training is the one in How a machine learns). The underlying idea is the same: look for the numbers that make the error smallest. Predicting is using the line with an x that was not in the data. Open the same tool with the prediction at x = 4: the green point on the line and the reading x = 4 → y = 4.407. There is nothing more behind it: a prediction is the height of the line at that point. The name of all this, regression, also has a history. It comes from a study by Francis Galton in 1886 about heights. Galton compared each child’s height with the mean of their two parents’ heights, and saw that the children strayed from the population’s average height less than their parents did: if the mean of the two parents was, for example, 6 cm above the average, the children also tended to be above it, but only about 4 cm: closer to the average. The same happened below the average with short parents. He calculated that the children stayed at around two thirds of their parents’ distance from the mean: they “regressed” toward it (Regression toward the mean, on Wikipedia). The name stuck for the method even though it has nothing to do with going backward. The classic mistake You might think a model understands the data. The […]
