items.title: WebAIAssist: One Assistant for the Agentic Web
items.summary: Author(s): Andrei Besleaga (Nicolae) Originally published on Towards AI. A free, open-source Chrome extension that puts an AI helper in your side panel, with a local AI model running in your browser, lets it use the tools any web page offers, and interact with websites by chat. Web pages are learnin
items.content: Author(s): Andrei Besleaga (Nicolae) Originally published on Towards AI. A free, open-source Chrome extension that puts an AI helper in your side panel, with a local AI model running in your browser, lets it use the tools any web page offers, and interact with websites by chat. Web pages are learning to talk to AI assistants. With WebMCP, a page can say: here is what you can do on me, and here is how to ask. Search this catalogue. Read this article. Check this order. Search for Flights. There is a catch. A page that offers tools needs an assistant that can use them, and you should be the one who chooses that assistant. WebAIAssist is built to be that assistant for any page. It is a chat interface in Chrome’s side panel. It runs a small AI model on your own computer (or remote models if you have accounts and API keys), lists the tools the open page offers, and asks you before it uses any of them. On a page with no tools, it can still read the page and answer your questions about it. It is free and open source (Apache-2.0). There is no account and no analytics. You can install it from the Chrome Web Store. WebMCP in one minute An AI assistant can use a website in two ways. It can look at the screen and click around like a person, which is slow and breaks whenever the layout changes. Or the page can hand it a list of tools. WebMCP is the second way. A page registers its tools, each with a name, a description, and the inputs it accepts. An assistant running in the visitor’s own browser can then call a tool directly instead of guessing where to click. It is still a draft. The W3C Web Machine Learning Community Group is incubating it, with editors from Google and Microsoft. It is not a W3C standard, and it may change. In Chrome, you turn it on with a switch, which I explain below. What WebAIAssist does It works on any site with WebMCP tools. It is not tied to my own projects. Open a page, allow the site, and the panel lists the page’s tools with their descriptions and shows which ones only read data. You approve every call. Before a tool runs, the panel shows the tool, the site, and the exact arguments, and waits for you to press Allow once. You can let read-only tools skip the prompt for one site in one session, but tools flagged for review always ask. The extension never clicks, navigates, or fills in forms by itself. The model runs on your computer. You can pick a small model that runs on your graphics card (Qwen3 0.6B, Qwen3.5 2B, Llama 3.2 3B, or Gemma 4 E2B), one that runs on your processor (Qwen3 0.6B, Qwen3 1.7B, or Qwen3.5 2B), or Chrome’s built-in Gemini Nano. With these, your questions and the page text are not sent to a model service. The model files are downloaded once (about 350 MB to 2.8 GB for the first one). Or bring your own model. Point the panel at a local server such as Ollama or LM Studio, or at a remote OpenAI-style service like OpenRouter. With a remote service, your questions, the tool list, the tool results, and the page text you read go to that host. The panel asks you once for each host before connecting. It helps on ordinary pages, too. On a page with no tools, Read this page gives the model the page text to answer from. A site that says no to AI input in its robots.txt is respected: the model gets no text from it. Zero access by default. The extension is granted no site access at install. You allow one site at a time. It shows what a site says to machines. The panel reads and displays files such as llms.txt, robots.txt, and security.txt. Try it in two minutes You need Chrome 126 or newer (processor models require Chrome 137 or newer), or another Chromium browser. Install WebAIAssist from the Chrome Web Store. Enable WebMCP. Open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing, set WebMCP for testing to Enabled, and relaunch Chrome. Without this switch, pages cannot show their tools. Open the side panel and pick a model. The first one downloads once. Open a page that offers tools, for example any page on agenticsystemcore.com, and allow the site. Ask a question. When the model wants to call a tool, read the call and press Allow. A site built for it: AgenticSystemCore 1.1 An assistant is only as useful as the tools a page gives it. So, here is the other half of my work. AgenticSystemCore is an open specification with a reference engine. It turns a folder of Markdown notes into a website, a knowledge graph, and files that agents can read. I released version 1.1.0 on 13 November 2026. It is a first that can gather and publish formatted texts as knowledge in a standard way, and could be used in multiple scenarios and types of work (such as: distributed second brain, auto-wiki with ontologies, nodes of semantic web and agentic knowledge web, collaborative project board, knowledge website, agentic system architecture, and other usages between agents and humans). Every page of a site built with it registers the same ten tools for WebMCP. They read, search, and cite. A change comes back as text for a person to merge. On these sites, WebAIAssist also adds a graph explorer and a read-only SPARQL view for ontology queries between documents. These same ten tools are available outside the browser through an MCP server for desktop assistants. I tested that the two paths agree. Version 1.1 is a new version, meaning a folder that was valid under 1.0 stays valid. Besides the tools, it adds: Stated meaning for every link. For each kind of link, the specification now defines its inverse, whether it carries along a chain, and what […]

items.title: Google’s Gemini Decisions API Compared With Microsoft Decision 1, Jev, and OpenAI
items.summary: Last Updated on November 18, 2026 by Editorial Team Author(s): Yaroslav Originally published on Towards AI. Illustration generated with AI. On November 11, Google released the Gemini Decisions API and the model behind it, Gemini Decision 1. You give it evidence and a fixed question. It can estimate
items.content: Last Updated on November 18, 2026 by Editorial Team Author(s): Yaroslav Originally published on Towards AI. Illustration generated with AI. On November 11, Google released the Gemini Decisions API and the model behind it, Gemini Decision 1. You give it evidence and a fixed question. It can estimate the probability that a condition is true, choose from options you supply, or score something against a rubric. An app can use those answers to route a request or flag it for review. Google’s launch announcement · Decisions API documentation The part that caught my attention was the input. Gemini can evaluate text, images, audio, video, and PDFs. You can ask up to 1,000 independent questions about the same input in one request, within the context limit. Google AI Studio offers a playground and a free tier for prototyping. The paid rate is $0.10 per million input tokens, with no output-token charge. Gemini Decision 1 model card · Gemini API pricing Decision API inputs and pricing Microsoft Decision 1 accepts text or JSON through Microsoft Foundry, with a listed rate of $0.042 per million input tokens. When I tried it for UI checks, I struggled with the cases where the evidence I needed was visual. For decisions based on structured state or text, Foundry still appeals to me because it also offers models from OpenAI and Anthropic. Microsoft Decision 1 docs · Microsoft pricing announcement · Foundry model catalog TypeSafe’s Jev also lists $0.042 per million input tokens. I couldn’t attach images in the setup I tried, and bringing in a separate provider for one model felt like a lot of work for a company. TypeSafe now offers experimental image input, and Jev 1.14 can return a bounding box around a target in an image. OpenRouter also offers Jev and Gemini Decision 1, which gives teams already using it another way to compare them. TypeSafe’s release · Jev pricing · Jev on OpenRouter · Gemini Decision 1 on OpenRouter OpenAI’s Decisions API is generally available with GPT-6 Luna. It accepts text, images, and JSON and supports up to 400 questions per request. An image can be shared across the request or attached to an individual question. The API also supports prompt caching, with a listed rate of $0.10 per million uncached input tokens before applicable adjustments. All four APIs list zero charges for output tokens. OpenAI Decisions API documentation Author-created chart. Direct media inputs listed in the provider documentation on November 17, 2026. Google · Microsoft · TypeSafe · OpenAI Artificial Analysis Decision Index results The Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1 combines six evaluations covering document decisions, tool selection, knowledge, reasoning, and consistency when questions are rephrased. It weighs how confidently models answer alongside whether they get the answer right. Its tasks use text, so these scores tell us about decisions on that test suite. Image, audio, and video capability still needs its own evaluation. Decision Index · Methodology Index score, time per task, and estimated cost per million tasks Gemini Decision 1 via Google AI Studio · 66 · 211 ms · $345 Microsoft Decision 1 via OpenRouter · 62 · 274 ms · $143 Jev 1.14 via TypeSafe · 66 · 92 ms · $156 GPT-6 Luna (Decisions) via OpenAI · 60 · 206 ms · $339 Artificial Analysis snapshot, November 17, 2026. Scores are rounded. Time combines each evaluation’s median using the index weights. Cost is estimated for the benchmark’s tasks at listed prices. The Microsoft timing is for OpenRouter. Gemini · Microsoft · Jev · OpenAI Author-created chart. Time per task and estimated cost per million tasks for the routes measured by Artificial Analysis. Lower is better on both measures. Decision Index v2.1 Jev and Gemini rounded to the same score. Jev took less than half the time per task and cost less than half as much on this suite. For my own work, Gemini is still the one I’d try next when the evidence is an image or a recording. I can experiment in AI Studio alongside the other Gemini models, which makes it easier for me to justify trying a decision model in the first place. items.title: Let the LLM Read the Paperwork, Not Make the Decision
items.summary: Last Updated on November 18, 2026 by Editorial Team Author(s): Abivarma Originally published on Towards AI. For regulated eligibility checks on structured data, a tested rule in code wins, and the criterion is what an inconsistent answer costs. When a decision runs on structured data and fits in a r
items.content: Last Updated on November 18, 2026 by Editorial Team Author(s): Abivarma Originally published on Towards AI. For regulated eligibility checks on structured data, a tested rule in code wins, and the criterion is what an inconsistent answer costs. When a decision runs on structured data and fits in a rule, I keep it in deterministic code. A language model gets one narrow job at the edge: reading the input that isn’t structured. Image by the author. The rule decides every application; the model only extracts fields from the hardship letter, and validation stands between it and the decision.The article argues against “agentic washing” for regulated eligibility decisions, where a deterministic rule is repackaged as an LLM agent loop that increases cost, latency, and the risk of inconsistent answers. It lays out four architectural options (rules-only, one model call, a multi-agent loop, or rules with a narrow model extraction step) and evaluates them against criteria like what a wrong answer costs, whether inputs are already structured, whether logic can be expressed as rules, how changes can be validated, and per-decision cost/latency. The author’s recommendation is a hybrid design: deterministic code makes the decision every time, while the model is restricted to single-turn extraction from unstructured attachments (like hardship letters), followed by strict validation and routing failures to human review. The piece also covers tradeoffs (upfront engineering, the need for deterministic correctness, queue staffing, and organizational pressure), ownership boundaries across risk/policy, the eligibility service team, model/evaluation owners, operations for review queues, and a design review rule that prevents model outputs from becoming the decision without passing deterministic checks. Finally, it provides a migration strategy for systems already using agents (shadow mode, measure costs/latency, move arithmetic off agents, validate before writes) and states the condition that would reopen the decision: when inputs stop being structured, policy can’t be enumerated, tolerance changes, or the review queue becomes burdensome. items.content: Collecting large-scale, diverse, and high-quality post-training datasets for autoregressive language models is challenging. Consequently, Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) is typically applied to datasets significantly smaller than those used for pre-training, which leads to overfitting and the catastrophic forgetting of the tails of the data distribution. items.summary: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gate
items.content: Applications such as visual accessibility agents and robotics require answering questions about recent video content promptly, over a bounded window of past frames (e.g., the last two minutes). Hybrid vision-language models (VLMs), which interleave attention with linear recurrent layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), are attractive for this setting, but maintaining a sliding window is expensive. The reason is that recurrent layers combine all past frames into a shared state, so expiring old frames normally requires re-running the entire window through the model. We observe that the recurrent update is affine in the state with input-dependent coefficients, so the effect of each frame can be captured as a transformation that composes associatively. items.summary: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. items.content: We present a provably distortion-free semantic watermarking algorithm that requires only black-box sampling access to a generative model and black-box access to a semantic embedding. A watermark is called distortion-free if, averaged over its secret detection key, it leaves the generator's output distribution unchanged; this provides a formal guarantee that watermarking does not reduce output quality. Conventional such watermarks are often brittle to transformations. This is especially problematic for images, where benign operations such as compression, cropping, or resizing change the entire pixel representation. items.content: Vision-language models (VLMs) can provide harmful assistance by interpreting visual events, even without an explicit request for the underlying harmful objective. items.content: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. items.content: We investigate how language models process negation in natural language inference (NLI). We propose the \textit{Polarity Composition Hypothesis}, a high-level causal model of this computation. Behavioral evaluations show that language-model predictions largely conform to the proposed hypothesis. Using Distributed Alignment Search, we identify causally effective subspaces aligned with the variables in the polarity-composition hypothesis. These representations transfer across negation forms and partially to a subset of MNLI. We release the dataset and code.

items.content: Preference optimization (PO) is the standard way to reduce object hallucination in large vision-language models. We find that four public PO checkpoints of LLaVA-1.5-7B also lower object coverage. They name fewer object categories, and their lower hallucination rates bring no significant gain in set-level object F1 on CHAIR. We therefore ask how much of the PO gain the base model can reproduce by stopping earlier. A positive end-of-sequence (EOS) logit bias lets the base model reach the recall of each PO model, and this early stopping alone reproduces 58 to 86 percent of the CHAIRi gain of three checkpoints on two disjoint COCO sets. items.content: A working-memory model must remember stimuli and use its memory flexibly to perform different tasks. We train the model on five tasks, including remembering a sample while other images are presented, categorizing distractor images while remembering the sample, and determining whether an image is new or has been presented before. The same trained model performs all tasks, guided by explicit cues about which response is required. items.content: GRPO has become the dominant reinforcement learning method for eliciting reasoning capability in LLMs using verifiable rewards. However, it suffers from a fundamental failure mode: when a training question exceeds the base model's current capability, all generated responses fail and receive zero reward, yielding no gradient signal and stalling further capability expansion. An emerging class of GRPO extensions, termed Hint-Augmented GRPO (HA-GRPO), adds a "hint" to the context to reduce the difficulty of the question, thereby producing a usable gradient signal. items.content: Event cameras offer high temporal resolution and low power consumption, making them promising for speech-related applications. items.content: Generative Artificial Intelligence is transforming the role of natural language in computational systems. In classical Natural Language Processing (NLP), language was treated as an object of computation: something to analyse, classify, translate, or generate. Large Language Models (LLMs) challenge this perspective, enabling natural language to function increasingly as an executable cognitive medium through which humans structure reasoning, orchestrate problem solving, and regulate hybrid human/AI workflows. This paper introduces Natural Language Programming (NLPg) as a theoretical and epistemological extension of traditional NLP. items.title: Hidden-State Similarity Predicts Re-Elicitation After Inoculation Prompting
items.summary: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can rea
items.content: Fine-tuning on narrow harmful tasks can cause emergent misalignment, where models generalize harmful behavior beyond the training distribution. Inoculation prompting can reduce this effect by explicitly eliciting the undesired behavior during training, but recent work shows that the behavior can reappear when evaluation prompts contain cues from the training context. We study what makes such prompts effective triggers. We find that, surprisingly, textual similarity to the inoculation prompt is an incomplete predictor. Instead, prompts are more likely to re-elicit suppressed behavior when they induce activation states similar to those produced by the inoculation context. items.summary: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Mode
items.content: AI-assisted RTL localization and debugging need ground-truth bug datasets with known locations and observable failures, while testbench grading uses injected bugs to measure detection capability. Creating such datasets at scale remains a major EDA challenge. BugGen 1.0 shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate context-aware RTL mutations. Still, it relies on the model for both choosing where to mutate and generating the edit, which increases inference costs and can lead to invalid choices. BugGen 2.0 changes this division of labor. Deterministic algorithms handle structural analysis, target selection, and validation, while the LLM focuses on localized semantic rewriting. items.content: Transfer learning in reinforcement learning (RL) has shown strong empirical success. In this work, we take a more principled perspective by studying when and how transferring knowledge between MDPs (a source and a target) can be provably beneficial. Specifically, we consider the case where there exists an undo map such that applying this map to the target's state space recovers the source exactly. We propose an algorithm that learns this map by matching state feature statistics gathered from both MDPs, and then uses it to transfer the source policy to the target. items.title: Runtime Verification of Multiple Natural Language Criteria for Agent Governance
items.summary: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the share
items.content: AI agents are governed by hundreds of natural language criteria, yet existing verifiers cannot efficiently evaluate an agent's output against a large set of such criteria and report which are satisfied, violated, or inapplicable. We introduce the VFM, a tree-attention verifier that encodes the shared context and target text, and scores N natural language criteria in parallel, returning independent per-criterion ternary verdicts. The VFM is pretrained on CriteriaBank, a corpus of 394K (context, target, criterion, verdict) tuples spanning over 321K distinct criterion strings. A finetuned VFM-4B outperforms GPT-5.4 on a synthetic governance benchmark. items.title: The Resolution Hypothesis: Agent Evolution's Key Is Identifying Improvements
items.summary: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain ta
items.content: Agent evolution follows a simple loop: a proposer writes candidate artifacts (prompts, skills, memories) and selection accepts those that score higher. This loop has shown promise, yet practitioners face a puzzle: methods trade wins across papers, and evolution often fails to bootstrap on certain tasks. We trace this puzzle to the Resolution Hypothesis: agent evolution stalls not because methods fail to propose better artifacts, but because noisy evaluations cannot reliably identify them. Across seven evolution methods and six models (over 10M LLM calls), we find support for the hypothesis at both levels where evaluation scores are used.
